food.text: The Linear Pottery culture represents a major event in the initial spread of agriculture in Europe. It flourished c. 5500 to 4500 BC, with evidence found along the middle Danube, the Elbe and the Rhine.

Danubian I peoples cleared forests and cultivated fertile loess soils from the Balkans to the Low Countries and the Paris Basin. They kept domesticated cows, pigs, dogs, sheep and goats. Their settlements consisted of longhouses.

The Funnelbeaker culture introduced farming and husbandry as major food sources to the pottery-using hunter-gatherers north of its line. It grew out of a merger of local Neolithic and Mesolithic traditions between the lower Elbe and middle Vistula rivers.

Finds of barley and emmer at Michelsberg culture sites indicate an agricultural economy. Bones of domesticated cattle, pigs, sheep and goats point to animal husbandry, while deer and fox bones suggest hunting supplemented the diet.

At the Michelsberg site, some pits contained the remains of food stores. Researchers suggest the site may have been abandoned because the Rhine's arms dried up in an extensive dry period, leaving the area unable to easily support agriculture.

The Linear Pottery culture's characteristic tool was the shoe-last celt, a long thin stone adze used to fell trees and sometimes as a weapon. The skulls found at Talheim, Neckar in Germany and Schletz in Austria are evidence of this use. One theory, by Eduard Sangmeister, holds that its settlements were abandoned, possibly as fertile land was exhausted, then reoccupied perhaps once the land had lain fallow long enough.

art.text: The Linear Pottery culture flourished from about 5500 to 4500 BC across the middle Danube, the Elbe and the Rhine. Its pottery was made up of simple cups, bowls, vases and jugs without handles. Later versions gained pierced lugs, bases and necks.

The Baden culture made wagon-shaped models in pottery, sometimes with a handle, among the earliest such models known. Pairs of cattle were buried nearby, which have been read as draft animals. No real wagons have been found, but some scholars take the finds together as proof that wagons existed.

In one style of Linear Pottery, incised lines in the decoration are broken or ended by punctures, or strokes. These give the pattern the look of musical notes. This Musical Note pottery, called Notenkopfkeramik in German, appeared in Austria at about 5200 BC.

The Lengyel culture flourished from 5000 to 4000 BC and was centered on the Middle Danube. Its subgroups include the Austrian and Moravian Painted Ware I and II. Its pottery has turned up in western Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Austria, Poland and Slovenia.

The last phase of Linear Pottery was the Stroke-ornamented ware culture, called Stichbandkeramik in German, dated to 5000 to 4500 BC. It developed in central Europe and then spread eastward, moving down the Vistula and Elbe.

Baden burials in Slovakia and Hungary often placed the burned remains of the dead in anthropomorphic urns. Examples come from sites such as Slána and Ózd-Center. In Nitriansky Hrádok, a mass grave was also uncovered.

A second wave of the Danubian culture began around 4500 BC and used painted pottery with Asiatic influences. It superseded the first phase and was in turn followed by a third wave that used stroke-ornamented ware.

Long before the Nebra sky disc was made, earthworks such as the Goseck circle, dated to about 4900 BC, were already used to mark the solstices. The disc later carried this knowledge in the form of a portable object.

war.text: In 1983 a mass grave was discovered at Talheim, Germany, in a Linear Pottery Culture settlement, dating to about 5000 BC. It held the remains of 34 bodies: 16 children, nine adult men, seven adult women and two adults of indeterminate sex. All of the skeletons showed significant trauma that was likely the cause of death, and the evidence points to the first signs of organized violence in Early Neolithic Europe.

Near Schletz, about 33 kilometres north of Vienna, lies a mass grave that dates back about 7,500 years. The ditch could hold up to 300 people, and the remains of 67 have been uncovered, all showing multiple points of trauma. Scientists concluded these people were victims of genocide, killed by weapons characteristic of LBK peoples, so the attackers are believed to be members of other LBK tribes. It is one of the earliest known sites showing proof of genocide in Early Neolithic Europe.

Another Neolithic mass grave in Germany, at Schöneck-Kilianstädten, dates to 5207–4849 BCE and may show deliberate mutilation and/or torture. Its skeletons have a remarkably high percentage of long bones, especially in the lower leg, that were broken around the time of death. This suggests deliberate targeting of those parts of the body, possibly while the victims were still alive, and the grave has been called "indisputable evidence for another massacre".

At Talheim, all 34 skeletons showed significant trauma likely to have caused death: 18 skulls bore wounds from the sharp edge of LBK adzes, 14 from the blunt edge of adzes, and 2–3 from arrows. Several skeletons also showed repeated, healed-over injuries, though not all wounds had healed at the time of death. None showed defensive wounds, indicating the population was fleeing when it was killed. The head wounds indicate LBK weapons and all the skeletons resemble LBK settlers, so the violence most likely occurred among LBK populations themselves.

The Schletz site was enclosed, which serves as evidence of violent conflict among tribes. The people who lived there had built two ditches to counter the menace of other LBK communities. Such fortifications were built as a form of defense against aggressors.

At Schletz, as at Talheim, fewer women were found than men, in similar proportions. Because young women are scarce among the dead, it is possible that other women of the defeated group were kidnapped by the attackers. At Talheim, researchers theorized that women were captured rather than killed, and that capturing women may have been the primary motive for the fierce conflict.

science.text: The Funnelbeaker culture (c. 4100–2800 BCE) introduced farming and husbandry as major food sources to pottery-using hunter-gatherers in north-central Europe. It arose as a technological merger of local Neolithic and Mesolithic traditions between the lower Elbe and middle Vistula rivers.

The Linear Pottery culture flourished c. 5500–4500 BC and marked a major event in the initial spread of agriculture in Europe. It began on the middle Danube, including western Hungary, and was carried down the Rhine, Elbe, Oder and Vistula.

Funnelbeaker sites of the 4th millennium BC have yielded artefacts of arsenical bronze made by the lost-wax casting method. The culture also used copper, especially for daggers and axes. Evidence of copper smelting in Scandinavia dates from about 3500 BC.

A ceramic tureen from Bronocice in Poland is engraved with a covered carriage. It is indirectly dated to 3636–3373 BCE and is the oldest evidence for covered carriages in Central Europe. The pot is now in the Archaeological Museum of Cracow.

Funnelbeaker people used copper daggers and axes. Older beliefs placed the source of the copper in the Austrian Alps, but recent studies established that the early copper (4100–3000 BCE) was mined in Serbian and Bulgarian mines.
The Linear Pottery culture built timber trackways, and some remains have been preserved. One at the Campemoor bog in Lower Saxony, Germany, is dated to c. 4630 – c. 4550 BC.
Central Germany was a primary area of the Linear Pottery culture (c. 5500 BC – c. 4500 BC). During this period, Neolithic circular enclosures were built in Central Europe.
Artefacts of arsenical bronze are known from Funnelbeaker sites in the 4th millennium BC. They were made using the lost-wax casting method.

Many C-14 dates exist for the Linear Pottery culture, allowing statistical analysis. Stadler and Lennais set 68.2% confidence limits at about 5430–5040 BC, and the 95.4% confidence interval at 5600–4750 BC.

At Flintbek in northern Germany, cart tracks dating from about 3400 BCE were found underneath a megalithic long barrow. They are the earliest known direct evidence of wheeled vehicles in the world, as opposed to models or images.

culture.text: The Linear Pottery culture flourished c. 5500 to 4500 BC and marks a major event in the initial spread of agriculture in Europe. Its pottery was simple: cups, bowls, vases and jugs without handles. Later versions added pierced lugs, bases and necks.

The fortified settlement of Kapellenberg near Hofheim and Frankfurt, one of the largest of the Michelsberg culture, has been described as representing the beginnings of urbanism already in 4000 BC. The site was 45 hectares, with 26 hectares of settlement holding numerous rectangular houses inside a rampart.

The Funnelbeaker culture is named for its ceramic beakers and amphorae with funnel-shaped tops, found in dolmen burials. It introduced farming and husbandry as major food sources to pottery-using hunter-gatherers in the north.

At the centre of the Kapellenberg settlement, a large tumulus was built between 4200 and 4100 BC. It suggests the influence of the Castellic culture in Brittany, where giant burial mounds with megalithic tombs were built for elite males some researchers call divine kings.

The Michelsberg culture, dated c. 4400 to 3500 BC, lay along both sides of the Rhine and started the European tradition of timber framing. It is named after a hill near Untergrombach in Germany, and the German archaeologist Jens Lüning built its pottery chronology in the 1960s.

A ceramic tureen from Bronocice in Poland carries an engraving of a covered carriage, dated between 3636 and 3373 BCE. It is the oldest evidence for covered carriages in Central Europe, and the cattle drawing it were presumably oxen whose remains were found with the pot.

The Rössen culture, from 4,600 to 4,300 BC, is named after the necropolis of Rössen in Saxony-Anhalt and has been identified in 11 of the 16 states of Germany. It marks the transition from the earliest Neolithic LBK tradition toward the more diverse complexes of Michelsberg and Funnel Beaker.
Around 5200 BC a new style called Music Note Pottery (Notenkopfkeramik) appeared in Austria. It belonged to the Middle Linear Band Pottery culture and moved eastward into Romania and Ukraine.

The late phase of the Linear Pottery culture is known as Stroke-ornamented ware (Stichbandkeramik), dated 5000 to 4500 BC. It evolved in central Europe and then spread eastward, moving down the Vistula and Elbe.

Jade axes have been found at Kapellenberg, as they were in Brittany's Castellic mounds, where the jade was originally imported from the Italian Alps. They point to an exchange network of prestige goods linked to elites, as well as trade in salt.

At Flintbek in northern Germany, cart tracks from c. 3400 BCE were discovered underneath a megalithic long barrow. This is the earliest known direct evidence for wheeled vehicles in the world, meaning actual tracks rather than models or images.
In 2019, two large rondel complexes were discovered east of the Vistula near Toruń in Poland. They were found as part of the range of the Linear Pottery culture.

An engraving on a ceramic tureen from Bronocice in Poland is the oldest evidence for covered carriages in Central Europe, dated to between 3636 and 3373 BCE. The carriages were drawn by cattle, presumably oxen whose remains were found with the pot.
